lectures.name: Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature
lectures.title: Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature
lectures.framing: Body temperature is a regulated variable held by negative feedback: thermoreceptors report to the hypothalamus, which drives effectors that either produce or lose heat — every effector in the table below simply runs in one of two directions.
lectures.keypoints: Normal oral temperature = 37°C (35.5–37.7°C), and no single value is the upper limit of normal. Anterior hypothalamus = heat loss (front, fire); posterior = heat conservation (back, brrr). Circadian peak 2 PM, trough 4 AM. Each 1°C rise ↑ HR by ~4.4 bpm. Thermoregulation reaches adult levels after puberty (girls 13–14, boys 17–18).

blocks.html:
Context: four arms of the immune system that fight pathogens
  1. Antibodies and the cells that make them
  2. Complement
  3. T cells
  4. Non-specific effector cells

Pathogens = bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites.

Thermal compartments and normal values
  • Core = internal organs and muscles; shell = skin and subcutaneous fat
  • Temperature fluctuations in the periphery (shell) help hold the core constant
  • Normal oral temperature = 37°C (35.5–37.7°C) — no single temperature can be used as the upper limit of normal
  • Physiological variation: circadian rhythm (peak 2 PM, lowest 4 AM), menstrual cycle, post-menopausal hot flashes, fever
  • 1°C ↑ in body temperature = 4.4 bpm ↑ in HR
  • Thermoregulation reaches adult levels once puberty ends: girls 13–14 years, boys 17–18 years
The control loop
  • Negative feedback system: sensors → integrating centre → effectors
  • Thermoreceptors: sensory neurons activated by warmth or cold — in skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, brain
  • Hypothalamus integrates thermoreceptor input — anterior = heat (front, fire), posterior = cold (back, brrr)
  • Feedforward mechanism: the body acts in anticipation of thermal changes

lectures.name: Innate Immunity Refresher
lectures.title: Innate Immunity Refresher
lectures.framing: A refresher on the four arms that fight pathogens — antibodies and B cells, complement, T cells, and non-specific effector cells — organised around one idea: innate recognition (PRRs, complement) starts inflammation, and antigen-presenting cells hand it over to specific B and T cell responses.
lectures.keypoints: Fab binds antigen; Fc sets the function (phagocyte receptors, mast cells, C1) — class switch changes Fc, never specificity. IgM = first, pentameric, best at complement; IgG = most abundant, only one to cross the placenta; IgA = mucosal dimer; IgE = mast cells, type I hypersensitivity, helminths. Classical and alternate complement pathways converge on C3; C3a/C4a/C5a = anaphylatoxins, C3b = opsonin, C5b–C9 = MAC. MHC I → CD8+, all nucleated cells; MHC II → CD4+, APCs only. IL-1 and TNF-α are endogenous pyrogens; IL-6 → CRP.

blocks.html:
Sequence of the innate inflammatory response
  • Clotting factors activate cleavage of complement into reactive subunits that act on local innate cells and the vasculature (initially restricted)
  • Local mast cells and tissue macrophages recognise molecular patterns via pattern recognition receptors (PRR), e.g. toll-like receptors (TLR)
    • PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns): bacterial lipopolysaccharide, CpG motifs
    • DAMPs (damage-associated molecular patterns): molecules released in response to tissue damage
  • Mast cell activation → histamine → ↑ permeability (tumor, dolor) and vasodilation (rubor, calor)
  • Blood flows into the injured area; plasma containing antibodies and complement flows out into the tissue
  • Macrophage activation → cytokines and chemokines → other leukocytes attracted
    • Cytokines alter expression of adhesion molecules on vascular endothelium
    • Key cytokines: TNF, IL-1; key chemokines: IL-8, C3a
  • Neutrophils, T cells and more macrophages flood the site
  • Local dendritic cells, made phagocytic by the inflammation, take up digested bacterial material and travel to the draining lymph node → present antigen to T cells and provide antigen for B cell uptake

blocks.html:
Antibodies: structure
  • Antibodies / immunoglobulins recognise specific antigen and bind pathogens to bring them to the attention of the rest of the immune system (complement, phagocytes)
  • Four polypeptide chains held by disulphide bonds
    • 2 identical heavy chains — μ, δ, γ, α, ε
    • 2 identical light chains — kappa, lambda
  • Fab region = N-terminal ends of light + heavy chains → antigen binding
    • Hypervariable area encoded by gene elements that undergo random rearrangement, 5′ to 3′: 300–1000 variable heavy (VH), 13 diversity heavy (DH; heavy only), 4 joining heavy (JH), constant (C)
    • Young B cells undergo immunoglobulin gene rearrangement (splicing, deletion, recombination into one gene sequence) → great structural diversity to recognise any antigen the body meets
  • Fc region = C-terminal ends of heavy chains → biological activity
    • Binds receptors on phagocytes → phagocytosis
    • Binds Fc receptors on mast cells before the antibody meets antigen
    • Binds complement → starts complement activation

blocks.cap: Antibody structure: two heavy and two light chains; the Fab (antigen-binding) arms and the Fc stem.

rows: Pathogens tagged for destruction by macrophages and neutrophils: Fab binds antigen on the pathogen, Fc binds receptors on the phagocyte

blocks.html:
B cell development: pre-B → naïve B
  • A functional B cell needs a functional antibody on its surface; B cells develop from stem cells in the bone marrow
  • Pre-B cells rearrange the heavy-chain gene, pair it with surrogate light chains and bring it to the surface
  • The heavy chain passes if the composite molecule activates Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) — allelic exclusion; failure → pre-B cell death, with a second chance on the other allele
  • Successful light-chain rearrangement → surface IgM and IgD → mature naïve B cell
Naïve B cells (have not yet seen antigen)
  • Enter the circulation and travel to lymphoid organs
  • Each naïve B cell carries a different antibody; one cell has hundreds of thousands of identical antibodies, all binding the same site on the antigen
  • After surface IgM, a B cell can class switch — changes the Fc, NOT the Fab → changes class and function, not antigen specificity
  • In lymph nodes, naïve B cells may meet the antigen their surface antibody recognises
  • >99% never encounter antigen and die within a few days
B cell activation
  • B cells recognise native, soluble antigen — unlike T cells, which need antigen processed and presented on MHC by an APC
  • Contact with antigen activates the B cell → receptor-mediated endocytosis of antibody + antigen in a vesicle
  • Digestive enzymes break antigen into peptides, which bind the open groove of MHC II on the vesicle membrane
T–B interaction, differentiation and secretion
  1. B cell presents antigen + MHC II to an activated CD4+ helper T cell (Th) specific for that antigen
  2. B and T cells form a conjugate; T cells release cytokines
  3. Cytokine signals (IL-4) drive B cell proliferation and differentiation
  • B cells: small lymphocytes, thin rim of cytoplasm; plasma cells: much larger, abundant ER and cytoplasm — produce and secrete antibody
  • Many B cells → plasma cells; a few → memory B cells; some daughters keep dividing
  • Plasma cells are the final stage of B cells that have recognised antigen and been stimulated by helper T cell cytokines; they secrete circulating antibody
  • Primary response (IgM, some IgG): first exposure — antibody levels take a few days to rise
  • Secondary response (IgG): persistent antigen or re-exposure — much faster and more robust
Memory B cells
  • The secondary response depends on long-lived memory B cells, generated in lymphoid tissue after activation and proliferation; reside in BM, lymph nodes, mucosal sites, spleen
  • High-affinity surface antibodies → activated by lower antigen levels than naïve B cells

blocks.html:
Antigens
  • Antigen: a substance able to induce a specific immune response — generates an antibody response
  • Usually foreign proteins entering via infection; sometimes the body's own proteins are treated as antigens
  • The pathogen itself is not an antigen — the proteins and carbohydrates that make up the pathogen are
  • One pathogen can carry thousands of molecules recognised as antigens — epitopes
  • Recognised by B cells (surface antibody) and T cells (T cell receptor)
  • Antibodies recognise antigen on bacterial/viral surfaces and free in the tissues

Complement: activation
  • A series of blood proenzymes converted to active enzymes by pathogens and by each other
  • Resembles the coagulation pathway — coagulation often activates complement
  • Classical pathway: C1, C4, C2, activated by the Fc regions of IgG or IgM after antibody has bound antigen
  • Alternate pathway: Factor B, D and P (properdin), directly activated by certain pathogens
  • Both converge on C3 → C3a + C3b
    • C3a: activates mast cells → local permeability and vasodilation; chemotactic for phagocytes
    • C3b: binds foreign organisms/immune complexes and tags them for phagocytes; reacts with C5–9 to form the MAC
The four outcomes
  1. Local vasodilation and ↑ vascular permeability — C3a, C4a, C5a = anaphylatoxins
    • Bind receptors on mast cells and basophils → degranulation → histamine and other mediators
    • Arteriolar smooth muscle dilates → more blood to local capillaries
    • More permeable endothelium → more fluid, IgG and complement
  2. Attraction of immune cells, especially phagocytes — C3a, C5a, chemokines
    • Chemotaxis: an immune cell is attracted to and moves toward a soluble factor
    • Chemokines: soluble proteins that attract cells to a site
    • Phagocytes are recruited to ingest organisms, antigens and inflammatory debris
    • Immune cells do NOT simply leak out with ↑ permeability like plasma proteins and water — they must be attracted by chemotaxis and cross the endothelium (transmigration)
  3. Opsonisation for phagocytosis — IgG, C3b
    • Opsonisation: particles/microorganisms coated with molecules that bind specific phagocyte receptors
    • C3b binds non-specifically to organisms/immune complexes; phagocytes carry C3b receptors (CR3) → bind, ingest, degrade
  4. Killing by the membrane attack complex (MAC) — C5b, C6, C7, C8, C9
    • C5 convertase splits C5 → C5a (diffuses away; anaphylatoxin, chemotactic) + C5b (binds the target, docking site for the rest)
    • C5b degrades quickly unless C6 binds (C5b6), then C7 binds; C7 changes conformation so the complex can insert into lipid membranes
    • C8 and C9 bind → MAC; C5b678 binds up to 16 C9 molecules
    • MAC = hydrophobic tube with a central pore (like a straw) → ions, water and small molecules pass freely → loss of osmotic integrity → rapid death

blocks.lead: Major histocompatibility complex — human MHC proteins = human leukocyte antigens (HLA)
rows: α chain + β chain, with a transmembrane segment anchoring them to the cell surface
Samples the cell's internal contents for the immune system; everyone's MHC differs (except identical twins), so self can be told from foreign
Presents antigen to helper T cells → both humoral (antibody) and cell-mediated immunity

blocks.html:
T cell receptor
  • TcR = α and β chains, associated with CD3 (a group of 5 linked proteins)
  • Like antibody, it has a variable region (by gene rearrangement) and a constant region
  • TcR complex = α chain + β chain + CD3
  • The TcR will NOT bind free antigen
T cell development in the thymus
  • A functional T cell needs a TcR that recognises peptide in the groove of self MHC and is linked to CD3 for signalling
  • Pre-T cells arise from lymphoid stem cells in the bone marrow and travel in the blood to the thymus
  • The α chain undergoes rearrangement and is brought to the surface with a surrogate α chain and tested (as written in source)
  • If it links to the signalling components → β-chain genes rearranged → mature TcR; the cell is now CD4+ CD8+ (double positive)
  • Test of self-MHC recognition on MHC-bearing thymic cells:
    • Binds weakly → continues development
    • Does not bind → no survival signal → dies (most cells)
    • Binds very strongly (self-peptide + self-MHC is its antigen) → killed
  • Survivors lose CD4 or CD8 → naïve CD4+ helper or naïve CD8+ cytotoxic T cell

blocks.html:
Antigen-presenting cells (APC)
  • Functionally defined cells that take up antigen and present it to T cells in the groove of MHC II
  • APC internalises antigen, processes it into peptides (lysosomal enzymes), and expresses the peptide on its surface
  • Dendritic cells are the most efficient — leave the infection site and travel to the lymph node
  • Macrophages and B cells can present to activated and memory T cells
Helper T cell (Th) activation
  • Starts with TcR–CD3 binding antigen–MHC II on an APC → biochemical cascade → T cell growth and proliferation
  • Mainly via ↑ IL-2 secretion and ↑ IL-2 receptors on the same cell — IL-2 is a potent autocrine growth cytokine driving clonal proliferation and differentiation
  • All progeny share the identical TcR, so recognise the same epitope; naïve bystander T cells have no IL-2 receptors and are not involved
  • Aided by CD4 and accessory molecules (CD45, CD28, CD2)
  • APC gives a co-stimulatory second signal through B7 (CD28:CD80/86) plus cytokines (IL-1, IL-12)
  • Activated Th cells become effector cells and help B cells become plasma cells
  • Th1: induced by IL-12, IFN-γ; secretes IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF-β → autoimmune responses, cell-mediated immunity
  • Th2: induced by IL-4; secretes IL-4, IL-5, IL-6 → IgE/eosinophil responses, humoral immunity
Cytotoxic T cell (Tc) activation
  • TcR on the CD8+ cell binds processed antigen on MHC I of an APC
  • Needs cytokine stimulation — IL-2 from nearby activated Th cells or self-produced
  • Resting Tc lack IL-2 receptors; antigen stimulation induces them, so only antigen-specific cells proliferate
  • Activated Tc → cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) that kill pathogen-infected self-cells (not pathogens themselves):
    1. Conjugate formation between CTL and target cell
    2. Membrane attack: cytokines, enzymes and perforin released from CTL granules by exocytosis
    3. Target cell death: granzyme enters the target and activates a caspase suicide pathway → apoptosis
  • CTL also express Fas ligand (FasL), which binds Fas on the target → caspase pathway

blocks.html:
Cytokines: general properties
  • Protein messengers made by immune cells to communicate and orchestrate the attack; maintain normal growth, migration and survival of immune cells
  • Include chemokines, interleukins and growth-factor subfamilies
  • The same cytokine may be made by many cell types
  • Pleiotropy: one cytokine, different effects in different circumstances
  • Redundancy: different cytokines, same activity
  • Synergy: cytokines act together and amplify each other
  • Most act in a paracrine or autocrine fashion

lectures.name: Microbiology Lab
lectures.title: The Microbiology Laboratory
lectures.framing: How a specimen becomes a result: the lab's value depends on getting the right specimen, before antibiotics, to the lab fast, and then on choosing between direct methods (microscopy, culture, molecular, antigen) and indirect ones (serology).
lectures.keypoints: Collect specimens BEFORE antibiotics, from the site of infection, avoiding normal flora. Blood culture: volume is the most critical factor; catheter-drawn cultures contaminate more. Gram-positive = purple (thick peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid → TLR2); Gram-negative = pink (outer membrane, LPS → TLR4). Serology: IgM+ = acute/recent; IgG alone = immunity; a fourfold rise between acute and convalescent sera confirms. S. aureus is catalase+/coagulase+ in clusters; S. pyogenes is catalase–, β-hemolytic, in chains, and its M-protein drives rheumatic fever.

blocks.html:
What the lab is
  • Devoted to culturing, examining and identifying microorganisms
  • Team: medical microbiologist, manager, coordinator, laboratory technologists, laboratory assistants
  • Sections: bacteriology, virology, mycology, parasitology, serology, molecular
  • Role: diagnosis and treatment of infectious diseases, infection control, public health
Laboratory Test Information Guide (LTIG) lists
  • Test purpose and limitations; patient selection criteria
  • Timing of collection; optimal collection sites; approved collection methods
  • Transport medium, transport time and temperature; holding instructions if not transported immediately
  • Minimum acceptable volume; test availability; turnaround time; result reporting procedures
Rejection criteria
  • Unlabelled, mislabelled or incompletely labelled specimens
  • Quantity not sufficient
  • Improper transport medium or improper swab
  • Inappropriate handling (temperature, timing, storage)
  • Improper collection site for the test requested
  • Leakage from the transport container

rows: Positive identification, patient preparation, sample collection, sample integrity
Standardisation, operator competence, analysis, quality assurance

blocks.html:
Specimen collection
  • From the site of infection, in sufficient quantity for the tests requested
  • Collect BEFORE antibiotics are given
  • Avoid contamination with normal flora
  • Right number of specimens; appropriate swabs/containers
  • Deliver to the lab ASAP
  • Label accurately — identifiers and clinical information

rows: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), tracheal aspirate, nasopharyngeal swab (NPS)

blocks.html:
Blood culture
  • Volume of blood collected is the most critical factor
  • Disinfect the venipuncture site
  • Catheter-drawn cultures have a higher contamination risk
  • Never submit catheter tips without an accompanying venipuncture blood culture
CNS infection
  • Meningitis, encephalitis, focal parenchymal infection, CNS shunt infection, subdural empyema, epidural abscess
  • Routes: hematogenous, direct spread from an infected site, anatomic defects in CNS structures, nerves
  • Ix: culture; molecular (viral — enterovirus, herpesvirus); antigen detection (fungal — cryptococcus)
  • Obtain blood cultures if meningitis is suspected
  • Tell the lab if unusual organisms are suspected
  • Collect 3–4 tubes of CSF by LP for bacterial culture and molecular testing — as much sample as possible
Respiratory infection
  • Mechanisms: aspiration, inhalation (aerosols, mycobacteria/TB), hematogenous seeding
  • Specimens: sputum, tracheal aspirate, blood culture, urine, serum, bronchial, pleural fluid, biopsy
  • Ix: clinical (signs and symptoms), radiographic (consolidation), microbiology (culture, molecular, antigen detection, serology)

rows: Influenza A and B, RSV, adenovirus, metapneumovirus, enterovirus, parainfluenza 1/2/3/4, rhinovirus, bocavirus, coronavirus
Cough, fever, CXR infiltrate; variable clinical features
Age, comorbidities (pulmonary, cardiac, liver disease), preceding influenza, alcohol abuse, immunosuppression (HIV, steroids)
ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, aspiration risk (dysphagia), microbial colonisation, ↑ gastric pH, immunosuppression, poor glycemic control

blocks.html:
Gastroenteritis
  • Ix: culture (bacterial), PCR (viral), ova and parasites, Clostridium difficile test

Skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs)
  • Primary cutaneous infections: cellulitis, ecthyma, impetigo, folliculitis, furunculosis, erysipelas
  • Do not use the label "wound" alone
  • Specimen of choice: biopsy of the advancing margin of the lesion
  • Do not ask the lab to report everything that grows
Antimicrobial susceptibility
  • Susceptibility testing: produces susceptibility profiles and detects resistance to therapeutic agents
  • Standardisation optimises bacterial growth and conditions and keeps results reproducible
  • Breakpoint: MIC or zone-diameter value used to categorise S, SDD, I, R, NS
  • Interpretive category: derived from microbiological characteristics, PK-PD parameters and clinical outcome data

rows: Inhibited by usually achievable concentrations at the recommended dose for the site of infection

MIC approaches attainable blood/tissue levels; response may be lower than for susceptible isolates; implies efficacy where the drug is physiologically concentrated or when a higher-than-normal dose can be used
Not inhibited by usually achievable concentrations with normal dosing

blocks.lead: Diagnostic methods — direct methods show the organism; indirect methods show the host's antibody.
rows:
Magnifies objects too small for the naked eye; characterises cultivated organisms
Types: light, fluorescence, dark field, electron
Uses: rapid preliminary/final identification, detecting several organisms in one specimen or ones hard to culture, evaluating specimens, judging clinical significance, pre-culture information, choosing further tests

Multiplies organisms in medium under controlled conditions
Media: liquid = broth, solid = agar plate; nutritive (general purpose), enrichment, selective, differential
Colony shape: punctiform (pinpoint), circular, filamentous, irregular, rhizoid, curled · elevation: flat, raised, convex, umbonate, umbilicate, growth into media · margin: entire (smooth), irregular, filamentous
Identification: phenotypic, molecular, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry
Followed by antimicrobial susceptibility testing

Direct analysis of nucleic acid sequence — amplification or non-amplification
PCR: denature (95°C) → anneal (68°C) → elongate (72°C)
Use when: 1–2 pathogens cause most infections, no further characterisation needed, no reliable method exists, reliable methods are slow, or burden must be quantified
Advantages: detects nonviable, unculturable, fastidious, slow-growing or previously unknown organisms; quantifies burden
Disadvantages: detects only primer-targeted organisms; no isolate for further characterisation; false negatives; cannot tell colonisation from infection

Interpretation: change between acute and convalescent sera, fourfold rise in titre, cross-reacting antibodies

Bacteria: cell wall

  • Peptidoglycan = N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) + N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc)
  • MurNAc carries a pentapeptide; cross-links between D-Ala in one strand and lysine (Gram-positive) or mDAP (Gram-negative) in the next give the wall its rigidity

lectures.name: The Normal Healthy Microbiome
lectures.title: The Human Microbiome
lectures.framing: The same microbe can be harmless or pathogenic depending on where it is: the organising idea is the spectrum from commensal → coloniser → infection, plus dysbiosis when the community itself shifts.
lectures.keypoints: Commensal = usual habitat; coloniser = unusual habitat, no disease; infection = wrong compartment or outside invader causing disease; dysbiosis = changed composition, diversity or metabolites. Most infections here are a compartment breach by the site's own flora (cellulitis, peritonitis, PID). Normally sterile: bladder, blood, CSF, lower respiratory tract.

Definitions
  • Human microbiome: the bacteria, archaea, fungi, parasites and viruses living in and on the body
  • Microbiota: the microorganisms found in a specific environment
  • Commensal: microbe in its usual habitat
  • Coloniser: microbe in an unusual habitat, not causing disease
  • Infection: microbe in a site causing disease (wrong compartment or unusual invader)
  • Dysbiosis: a change in the composition, diversity or metabolites of the microbiome
Sterile sites (and the infection when breached)
  • Bladder (urobiome), bloodstream (bacteremia), CSF (meningitis), lower respiratory tract (bronchitis, pneumonia)

lectures.name: Approach to a Patient with Fever
lectures.title: Approach to a Patient with Fever
lectures.framing: A fever workup runs in a fixed order — safety, then stability and sepsis screen, then history, exam, differential, investigations and treatment — with the thresholds and the history shifting by age group (children, adults, older adults).
lectures.keypoints: Screen for sepsis first: qSOFA ≥ 2 (RR ≥ 22, BP ≤ 100/60, altered mentation) in adults; SIRS ≥ 2 in pediatrics. Fever: 38°C in children; 37.2°C (6 AM) or 37.8°C in adults; in older adults 37.8°C once, 37.2°C persistent, or ≥ 1.1°C above baseline — and fever is absent in 30–50% of frail older adults with infection (look for falls, delirium). Always send 2 sets of blood cultures. Positive urine culture ≠ UTI; no urinalysis in patients over 65.

lectures.framing: E. coli shows how one species causes different diseases by which adhesin it carries and which toxin it secretes; mycobacteria, by contrast, are defined by a mycolic-acid wall that makes them acid-fast and drives chronic infection.

lectures.framing: Acute inflammation takes four morphological patterns, and what distinguishes them is what leaks out of the vessels: pus (neutrophils), fibrin, cell-poor fluid, or a breach of the mucosa itself.
lectures.keypoints: Purulent = pyogenic bacteria (Staphylococcus) → liquefactive necrosis; an abscess is walled off and avascular, so antibiotics penetrate poorly — drain it. Fibrinous = marked permeability lets fibrinogen out (e.g. fibrinous pericarditis: post-MI/Dressler's, cardiac surgery, uremia, SLE). Serous = cell-poor fluid: effusion, ascites, blister. Ulcer = a local mucosal defect.

lectures.framing: Clostridia are anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli, and each species is best remembered by what its toxin does — from colitis (C. difficile) to spastic (tetanus) or flaccid (botulism) paralysis.
lectures.keypoints: Spores are metabolically inactive and hard to destroy. C. difficile: TcdA/TcdB (TcdB most potent) + binary toxin CDT (CDTb pore, CDTa ribosylates actin) → pseudomembranous colitis; diagnose by NAAT or ELISA, not culture. C. perfringens → gangrene.

lectures.name: How Viruses Work
lectures.title: Viruses, Fungi, Parasites and Prions
lectures.framing: A survey of the non-bacterial agents. For viruses the organising idea is that the genome defines the virus — the Baltimore system classifies them by nucleic acid type and strand sense, and every virus runs the same seven-step replication cycle.
lectures.keypoints: mRNA is always the (+) strand; its complement is (–). Enveloped viruses bud through the host membrane and carry glycoproteins; naked viruses resist harsh conditions better. Replication: attach → enter → uncoat → translate → replicate genome → assemble → release. Fungal wall = mannoproteins, β-glucans, chitin; membrane = ergosterol. Parasites: cultures generally not an option — use smears, O&P, PCR, antigen. Prions are not microbes — misfolded proteins that template their shape.

blocks.html:
Viruses → acute and chronic infections
  • Viruses: infectious obligate intracellular parasites — DNA or RNA inside a protein coat and/or membrane
  • Virions: mature particles that can be released from the cell
  • Capsid: protein shell encasing the genome, held by non-covalent interactions; capsid + genome = nucleocapsid
  • Enveloped viruses: outer lipid bilayer acquired by budding through the host cytoplasmic membrane; glycoproteins on the envelope surface
  • Naked viruses: no envelope; often more resistant to harsh conditions
  • Morphology: helical, icosahedral (hollow, symmetrical, quasi-spherical), complex (non-symmetrical)
  • Virion components: polymerases, proteases, integrases, topoisomerases, capping enzymes, proteins, lipids
The genome defines the virus
  • It encodes gene products and signals for replication, assembly and packaging, timing of the replication cycle, modulation of host defences, and spread to other cells and hosts
  • mRNA is always the (+) strand; DNA of equivalent polarity is also (+)
  • Complements of (+) strands are (–) strands
Replication cycle
  1. Attachment to cell receptors
  2. Entry — penetration into the cytoplasm
  3. Uncoating — genome and contents released from the nucleocapsid
  4. Protein synthesis — translation of viral mRNA
  5. Genome replication — new genome copies
  6. Assembly of new virions
  7. Release — off to infect a new cell

lectures.title: Fever
lectures.framing: Fever is a raised hypothalamic set point driven by pyrogens and cytokines through PGE2 — which is exactly what separates it from hyperthermia, where the set point is normal and the body simply cannot shed heat.
lectures.keypoints: Fever: ≥ 37.2°C at 6 AM or ≥ 37.8°C any time (oral/tympanic). Exogenous pyrogen = LPS lipid A; endogenous pyrogens = IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ → PGE2 → set point ↑; cryogens limit it. FUO = ≥ 101°F on several occasions with a negative initial workup. Fever rarely exceeds 41°C and responds to antipyretics; hyperthermia can exceed 41°C and does not. Alarm features: very high fever, rash, altered mental status, dizziness, recent chemotherapy, dyspnea/chest pain.

blocks.html:
Definition

  • Benefits: inhibits growth of many microorganisms, ↑ antibody production, stimulates innate and adaptive responses
  • Common symptoms: rise in temperature (then sweating and falling temperature), chills, rigors; variable: headache, malaise, anorexia
  • Fever of unknown origin: ≥ 101°F documented on several separate occasions, with an appropriate initial workup failing to find the cause

lectures.name: Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1
lectures.title: Choosing Antibiotics Wisely
lectures.framing: Antibiotics are organised by the bacterial process they hit — cell wall, nucleic acid, protein or folate synthesis — and choosing one wisely means naming the syndrome, the target bugs, the narrowest empiric drug, then narrowing again when cultures return. The lecture closes on resistance, penicillin allergy, and the three big respiratory viruses.
lectures.keypoints: β-lactams bind PBPs (bactericidal) and are the safest antibiotics in pregnancy; carbapenems are the broadest and should be reserved. Vancomycin covers MRSA but is nephrotoxic; aminoglycosides (30S) are nephro- and ototoxic; fluoroquinolones carry tendon, aortic and CNS warnings — avoid when alternatives exist. > 90% of reported penicillin allergies are not true allergy; skin testing has > 95% NPV, and never challenge severe type II–IV reactions. MRSA = mecA/PBP2a; VRE = D-Ala-D-Lac. Drift → epidemic; shift (reassortment) → pandemic, and only influenza A shifts.

Resistance rising with overuse: β-lactamases hydrolyse the β-lactam ring before it reaches the target; PBP modification.

blocks.html:
Epidemiologic terms
  • Incubation period: exposure to first symptoms (unique for each disease)
  • Infectious period / period of communicability: when the agent can pass to another person; may start/stop before, during or after symptoms
  • Generation time: onset of infectiousness in a primary case → onset of infectiousness in the secondary case it infects
  • Basic reproductive number (R0): mean secondary infections from a typical case in a fully susceptible population — R0 > 1 outbreak continues (exponential growth); R0 < 1 outbreak ends
  • Effective reproductive number (R): the same in a mixed susceptible/non-susceptible population — R > 1 cases rise; R = 1 endemic; R < 1 cases decline
  • Antigenic drift: slow point mutations in one virus → may cause an epidemic
  • Antigenic shift: genetic elements of two viruses reassort into a new strain → may cause a pandemic

lectures.name: Intro to Infection Control
lectures.title: Introduction to Infection Prevention and Control
lectures.framing: Infection spreads along a six-link chain — agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host — and every IPAC measure works by breaking the weakest link. Additional precautions are chosen by the mode of transmission.
lectures.keypoints: Hand hygiene is the single most important infection-control measure — ABHR unless hands are visibly soiled (then soap and water). Droplets ≥ 5 μm travel < 2 m → mask + eye protection; airborne particles < 5 μm → fit-tested N95 + negative-pressure room (TB, measles, varicella, VHF). Doffing order: gloves, gown, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene. LHSC: alert level 1 = pre-outbreak, level 2 = outbreak (threshold met, health unit notified, admissions stopped).

blocks.html:
Transmission
  • Not all exposures lead to transmission and infection
  • Probability depends on host susceptibility, inoculum size, viability and virulence of the organism, and effectiveness of control measures
  • Herd immunity: when enough of a population is resistant, the few susceptible people are protected because the pathogen is unlikely to "find" them
  • Aerosol-generating medical procedures: intubation, manual ventilation, open endotracheal suctioning, CPR, bronchoscopy, sputum induction, nebulised therapy, autopsy, non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (CPAP)

lectures.framing: An AEFI is any unwanted health event within 6 weeks of immunisation, whether or not the vaccine caused it — so the lecture is about classifying causes, knowing the real (usually tiny) frequencies, and the mandatory reporting chain from provider to WHO.

lectures.name: Introduction to Sepsis
lectures.title: Introduction to Sepsis
lectures.framing: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection — inflammation that is no longer local. Management rests on four principles, and the one that saves the most lives is early, appropriate antibiotics.
lectures.keypoints: Mortality 30–40%; organ failure comes from microcirculatory dysfunction → MODS. Septic shock = hypotension that does not respond to fluids (arteriolar vasodilation + capillary leak) → add vasopressors. Every hour of antibiotic delay after hypotension ≈ 8% ↑ mortality — draw cultures first only if they will not delay antibiotics. Then find and control the source (drain, operate, remove the device); life support buys time but fixes nothing. Many targeted therapies (anti-TNF, activated protein C, anti-endotoxin, vitamin C…) have failed.

blocks.html:
What sepsis is
  • Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — bacteria, viruses or fungi
  • Common, deadly and an emergency — mortality 30–40%
  • Loss of balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators → cellular injury → multiple organ dysfunction (MODS); inflammation is no longer localised but systemic
  • Any organ can fail because of microcirculatory dysfunction in arteriolar–capillary networks:
    • Cardiovascular: ↓ BP, ↑ HR, myocardial dysfunction
    • Respiratory: hypoxia, ARDS
    • Brain; coagulation (thrombocytopenia, DIC); liver; kidneys; muscles; nerves
  • Septic shock: low BP that does not respond to fluids
    • Arterioles vasodilate and intravascular fluid leaks into the interstitium
    • Add vasoconstrictors to raise BP and avoid "salt-water drowning"/edema
  • Recognise it clinically — hypothermia or fever, tachycardia, ↑ RR, warm/flushed, ↓ BP — and look for the cause

lectures.name: Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance
lectures.title: Choosing an Antimicrobial Agent
lectures.framing: Choosing an antimicrobial means matching the likely organism and its likely susceptibility to host and drug factors — and deciding when to start, which depends on how sick the patient is.
lectures.keypoints: Septic shock, acute bacterial meningitis, febrile neutropenia → start immediately, with or right after specimen collection. Stable subacute infections (osteomyelitis, diskitis, subacute endocarditis) → collect samples first. Mild infections in healthy patients → no antibiotics unless the diagnosis is sure and bacterial. Indirect harms matter: disrupted bowel flora and selection of resistant pathogens. Oral options: fluoroquinolones, macrolides, clindamycin, doxycycline, TMP-SMX.

blocks.html:
What you need to know

  • Its susceptibility (or likely susceptibility), as accurately as possible
Host factors

Drug factors
  • Safety record, success record, microbial etiology, bactericidal vs bacteriostatic, penetration into the site, adverse effects
  • Direct adverse effects: neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity, DDIs, allergic reactions
  • Indirect adverse effects: effects on normal bowel flora; ↑ risk of infection with drug-resistant pathogens

lectures.title: Outbreak Management and Healthcare-Associated Infections
lectures.framing: Outbreak management follows ten ordered steps, from verifying that there is an outbreak to debriefing the team — and because outbreaks are sociological as much as medical, the fix must reach root causes.
lectures.keypoints: Reportable diseases are legislated: they feed surveillance, trigger the medical officer of health's authority, and meet Canada's International Health Regulations obligations. Case definition + line list (updated daily) + epidemic curve. Common source (point, continuous, intermittent) vs propagated (more than one incubation period). Isolation separates the sick; quarantine restricts the exposed. HAIs: 1 in 31 inpatients on any day; 35–55% preventable (most for CLABSI and CAUTI); 8,000 Canadian deaths/year.

blocks.html:
Principle
  • Outbreaks are sociological as much as medical phenomena — solutions must address root causes

blocks.html:
Healthcare-associated infections (HAI)
  • On any given day, 1 in 31 hospital patients has at least one HAI
  • 35–55% are preventable — highest for central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI) and catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI); lower for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and surgical site infection (SSI)
  • Each year 8,000 Canadians die from hospital-acquired infections; 220,000 more are infected
  • Treatment costs more than prevention ($129 million/year) — prolonged stays, special control measures, costlier drugs, extensive surveillance (MRSA)

lectures.name: Approach to the Immunocompromised Host
lectures.title: Approach to Fever in the Immunocompromised Host
lectures.framing: Different conditions impair different arms of the immune system, and immune deficiency is dynamic — it is all about timing. The differential is the usual one + opportunistic infections + context, remembering that the presentation (even the fever) may be blunted.
lectures.keypoints: Diabetes: ↓ C4, ↓ cytokine response, chemotaxis, killing and phagocytosis. Uremia: defective APC co-stimulation (poor hepatitis B vaccine response). HIV CD4 < 50 → MAC, CMV retinitis, lymphoma; > 500 → infections like the general population, plus TB. Allogeneic HSCT: neutropenia pre-engraftment → NK recovery → CD4 recovery late. Cytokine blockers can mask fever. Vaccinate — before immunosuppression where possible, and avoid live vaccines.

blocks.html:
Which condition, which defect
  • Diabetes mellitus: low C4; ↓ cytokine response after stimulation, ↓ chemotaxis, killing and phagocytosis
  • Renal failure: uremia → defective co-stimulatory function of antigen-presenting cells (thought to explain poor vaccine response, e.g. hepatitis B); ↓ lymphocyte numbers in dialysis patients
  • HIV: CD4 < 50 → M. avium, CMV retinitis, lymphomas; CD4 > 500 → infections similar to uninfected people, TB
  • High risk of invasive mould infection: chronic granulomatous disease, allogeneic HSCT, lung/heart transplant, AML/MDS
  • Immune deficiency is very dynamic — it is all about timing
Allogeneic stem cell transplant
  • Patient receives healthy donor stem cells to replace their own, which have been conditioned (radiation or high-dose chemotherapy)
  • Phases: pre-engraftment (neutropenia) → post-engraftment (NK cells recover) → late phase (CD4 T cells recover)

blocks.cap: After graft infusion, neutrophils, monocytes and NK cells recover within weeks; B and CD8 T cells over months; CD4 T cells take years.

blocks.html:
Approach
  • Fever may be absent on cytokine-blocking drugs: anakinra, rilonacept, tocilizumab, infliximab, golimumab, adalimumab
  • Build the differential around immune status: same differential + opportunistic infections + context
  • Presentation commonly differs between immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients
Prevention
  • Vaccination is imperative in immunocompromised patients; live virus vaccines are generally unsafe
  • Give vaccines before immunosuppressive medications when possible
  • Give antimicrobial prophylaxis to HIV patients and transplant recipients for infections with no vaccine

lectures.name: Opportunistic Infections
lectures.title: Opportunistic Infections
lectures.framing: Opportunistic infections occur more often and more severely when immunity is compromised. Five organisms anchor the lecture, and each is tied to a specific immune threshold or risk group.
lectures.keypoints: TB: airborne; 3 sputa (≥ 1 early morning); RIPE (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol). MAC: water sources, not person-to-person; disseminated at CD4 < 50; azithromycin + rifampin + ethambutol. CMV: 40–50% infected; reactivates at CD4 < 100 and in transplant; ganciclovir/valganciclovir, letermovir prophylaxis. Cryptococcus: meningitis; amphotericin B + flucytosine → fluconazole. PJP: CD4 < 200 or long-term steroids; ↑ LDH, ground glass; TMP-SMX ± steroids if severe.

lectures.name: Antifungals
lectures.title: Antifungals
lectures.framing: Fungi are eukaryotes, so selective drugs must hit what humans lack: the cell wall (echinocandins) or the ergosterol-based membrane (azoles block ergosterol synthesis; polyenes bind the membrane directly).
lectures.keypoints: Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (a CYP450) → no ergosterol; they also inhibit human CYP450s → drug interactions, plus QT prolongation and hepatotoxicity. Fluconazole is limited for non-albicans Candida. Echinocandins (caspofungin) block 1,3-β-D-glucan synthesis; reliable for Candida, few DDIs, IV only, poor eye/CNS/urine penetration. Amphotericin B is broad spectrum but nephrotoxic with infusion reactions.

blocks.html:
Why fungi are hard to treat
  • Fungi are eukaryotes and share more with human cells than bacteria do
  • Most drugs target the fungal cell wall, which humans lack
  • Ergosterol is the fungal equivalent of cholesterol, keeping the membrane stable across temperatures and environments; blocking its synthesis stops the fungus reproducing and surviving

lectures.name: Approach to Immunodeficiency
lectures.title: Approach to Immunodeficiency, Hypersensitivity and Allergy
lectures.framing: The pattern of infection points to the broken arm of immunity: phagocyte defects → catalase-positive bacteria and fungi; complement → Neisseria; T cells → opportunists in the first 6 months; antibodies → encapsulated bacteria after maternal IgG wanes. The second half turns the problem around — an immune system that overreacts (Gell and Coombs, anaphylaxis, common allergies).
lectures.keypoints: Secondary immunodeficiency is the commonest in practice. CGD = NADPH oxidase defect → catalase+ infections; DHR 123 assay. Terminal complement (MAC) deficiency → recurrent Neisseria. SCID is detected by TRECs on newborn screening and is fatal without BM transplant. Selective IgA = commonest humoral (mostly asymptomatic); CVID = commonest symptomatic (IgG replacement). Anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000, max 0.3 mg, repeat q5–15 min — everything else comes after. Introduce allergenic foods early (4–6 months).

blocks.html:

blocks.html:
HIV
  • Retrovirus that infects and destroys CD4 T cells → progressive loss of cell-mediated immunity
  • Spread by secretions (sexual intercourse), blood (shared needles, blood products), transplacental transfer
1. Initial infection
  • Virus enters cells; RNA reverse-transcribed into DNA, integrated into the host genome; particles assembled
  • Mild symptoms ~1 month after exposure
  • HIV-specific immune response → viral load falls, symptoms resolve
2. Clinical latency
  • Virus still replicates and destroys CD4 T cells; lasts ~8 years, asymptomatic
  • Long symptom-free survival possible, but ↑ cardiovascular disease, diabetes, renal disease, cancer
  • Treatment: combination drugs targeting different steps of viral replication
3. AIDS
  • Systemic symptoms and infections as in primary T-cell immunodeficiency: weight loss, lymphadenopathy, fever
  • Opportunistic infections (PJP), malignancy (Kaposi sarcoma)
  • Lasts ~2 years → death

blocks.html:
Anaphylaxis
  • A serious allergic reaction with rapid onset (minutes to within 1 hour) that may cause death
  • Lifetime prevalence 0.5–5%; 1% of ER visits for acute systemic allergic reactions are diagnosed as anaphylaxis
  • Caused by systemic release of mast cell and basophil mediators
Highly likely when ANY ONE of three criteria is met
  1. Sudden illness (minutes to hours) with skin/mucosal involvement (generalised hives, itch/flush, swollen lips-tongue-uvula) plus at least one of:
    • Sudden respiratory symptoms/signs (dyspnea, wheeze, cough, stridor, hypoxemia)
    • Sudden ↓ BP or end-organ dysfunction (hypotonia/collapse, incontinence)
  2. Two or more of the following, suddenly after exposure to a likely allergen/trigger:
    • Skin or mucosal symptoms
    • Respiratory symptoms
    • ↓ BP or end-organ dysfunction
    • GI symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, vomiting)
  3. ↓ BP after a known allergen:
    • Infants/children: low age-specific systolic BP or > 30% fall in systolic BP
    • Adults: systolic < 90 mmHg or > 30% fall from baseline
Treatment
  • Remove the trigger
  • Prompt IM epinephrine — 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 solution, max 0.3 mg; repeat every 5–15 min PRN
  • Other drugs only after epinephrine: O2, fluids, antihistamine, salbutamol, corticosteroids
  • Mean time to cardiorespiratory arrest: iatrogenic 5 min, insect sting 15 min, food 30 min

lectures.name: Approach to Allergy
lectures.title: Approach to Allergy Testing and Autoimmunity
lectures.framing: Allergy tests only mean something in the light of the clinical history — the best allergy test — because interpretation rests on pre-test probability and likelihood ratios. The lecture then turns to autoimmunity as a breakdown of tolerance, with rheumatoid arthritis as the worked example.
lectures.keypoints: History is the best allergy test; oral challenge is the gold standard. LR+ = Sn/(1–Sp); LR– = (1–Sn)/Sp. Skin prick or intradermal: positive = wheal ≥ 3 mm over the negative (saline) control, with histamine as positive control; intradermal is for drugs and venom. Cross-reactivity needs ~70% homology. Tolerance is central (deletion in BM/thymus) and peripheral (ignorance, anergy, deletion, Treg suppression). RA: HLA-DRB1 shared epitope binds citrullinated self-proteins → ACPA; smoking and periodontal disease (P. gingivalis) are risk factors.

blocks.html:
Principles of allergy testing
  • Testing helps diagnose type I hypersensitivity
  • The best allergy testing tool is the clinical history
  • Sensitivity and specificity differ by allergen and test type
  • Interpret using pre-/post-test probability and likelihood ratios, in the context of the history
  • Pre-test probability: clinical impression of the chance of a diagnosis — clinical experience, epidemiology, comorbidities, risk factors, exam findings
  • Likelihood ratio (LR): how much more likely a result is in someone with the disorder than in someone without it
    • LR+ = Sn / (1 – Sp): odds of a positive test in someone with the condition vs someone without
    • LR– = (1 – Sn) / Sp: odds of a negative test in someone with the condition vs someone without
    • Calculate from Sn and Sp, or use a nomogram
  • Cross-reactivity: occurs with ~70% homology between antigens (tertiary structure conserved) — e.g. birch pollen-food syndrome → oral pruritus with almond
Test reagents
  • Food allergen proteins for skin prick and serum IgE tests are commercially prepared
  • Purified food protein: should contain all relevant allergens; amount of each varies batch to batch
  • Recombinant extract: known allergens made in bacterial vectors; contains major known allergens but not lesser-known ones (false negatives); can spike purified extracts with clinically important low-concentration allergens
  • Environmental allergens: dust mites (feces), cat/dog (dander), seasonal (pollen), mould (spores)

RAST (radioallergosorbent test)
  • Blood radioimmunoassay detecting allergen-specific IgE
  1. Extract proteins from the allergen
  2. Fix the extract to a solid-phase surface and send to the lab
  3. Add the patient's serum; wash it away, leaving bound IgE
  4. Add a marker and measure how much IgE is bound
  • Component-based IgE testing: pinpoints the specific proteins causing symptoms — a newer test to better predict food reactions and cross-reactivity and identify major food and aeroallergens

Oral challenge — the gold standard

  • High-risk patients: start with very low doses unlikely to cause a reaction; optimise comorbidities; avoid in pregnancy; β-blockers can interfere with treatment of a reaction; do it in hospital and consider an IV beforehand

blocks.html:
Immune tolerance
  • Immune tolerance: antigen-specific unresponsiveness to self-antigens
  • Central tolerance: immature self-reactive lymphocytes are negatively selected/deleted in the BM and thymus; those with low-affinity self-receptors enter the periphery
  • Peripheral tolerance (spleen, lymph nodes) handles mature self-reactive lymphocytes by:
    • Immunologic ignorance (anatomical barrier)
    • Anergy/inhibition (blocks CD28:CD80)
    • Deletion (Fas ligand)
    • Suppression (regulatory T cells — IL-10, TGF-β)
  • Autoimmunity: failure to recognise self-cells, with resulting destruction of them

Autoimmune disease: epidemiology and approach
  • Any organ system; ~100 diseases have an autoimmune etiology
  • 1 in 30 people affected; females more than males
  • Mostly chronic inflammation of unknown cause — genetic (polygenic; MHC II / HLA most strongly associated) and environmental (pollen, toxic exposures)
  • The best approach is to have it on the differential

blocks.html:
Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Cause unknown; 1% of the population, 3× more common in women
  • Risk factors: DRB1 shared-epitope gene, toxic exposure (smoking), infection (periodontal disease), defective immune regulation
  • Specific HLA-DRB1 alleles encode MHC II with a shared epitope (SE), which binds strongly to self-proteins modified by citrullination
  • MHC-SE is associated with anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA)

Workup and treatment
  • Needs clinical suspicion from history and exam
  • Ix: blood antibodies, biopsy, pathology stains for inflammatory markers, imaging, genetics
  • Tx: replace what is missing (levothyroxine, insulin) or suppress the immune response (rituximab)

lectures.name: Pathology of Chronic Inflammation
lectures.title: Chronic Inflammation, Granulomas, Herpesviruses and Fungi
lectures.framing: Chronic inflammation is inflammation that persists for weeks to months alongside attempts at repair, driven by macrophages and lymphocytes; its signature structure is the granuloma, the body's attempt to wall off what it cannot clear. The lecture then catalogues two persistent pathogen groups — latent herpesviruses and medically important fungi.
lectures.keypoints: Causes of chronic inflammation: persistent infection (TB), hypersensitivity (RA, asthma, IBD), chronic toxin exposure (silicosis, atherosclerosis). Granuloma = epithelioid macrophages ringed by T cells, ± Langhans giant cells and caseation. Rule out TB before immunosuppression. Herpesviruses are dsDNA and latent, reactivating with stress, fever, UV, immunosuppression: HSV-1/2 and VZV in ganglia, CMV in WBCs (commonest congenital infection in Canada), EBV in B cells (malignancy). Mucor/Rhizopus thrive in hyperglycemic, acidotic states; invasive Aspergillus → voriconazole.

blocks.html:
Granulomas
  • Granuloma: aggregate of macrophages surrounded by T lymphocytes, formed in chronic inflammation
  • Activated macrophages accumulate cytoplasm and resemble epithelium — epithelioid histiocytes; nuclei sometimes look like footprints in the sand
  • Macrophages may fuse into multinucleate giant cells (Langhans cells)
  • Often an attempt to contain something hard to eradicate — talc in IV drug use, sutures
  • White nodule with a chalky/cheesy centre — necrotising/caseating from hypoxia and free-radical injury
  • Common sites: lungs, lymph nodes, GI tract
  • Causes: mycobacterial (TB), fungal (histoplasmosis), bacterial (cat scratch disease); sarcoidosis, vasculitis, Crohn's disease, foreign body reaction, malignancy

blocks.title: Screen for TB before immunosuppression
blocks.html: Make sure the patient does not have TB before starting immunosuppressive treatment for a non-infectious condition — the granulomas containing it depend on an intact immune response.

Nasal polyps

Herpesviruses: latency
  • dsDNA viruses
  • Latent infection: asymptomatic period after acute infection; no replication; hidden from the immune system
  • Reactivation: latent → active (lytic) infection
    • Triggers: fever, microbial co-infection, UV light, stress, tissue injury, hyperthermia, hormonal imbalance, allogeneic stimulation, cytokines, cell differentiation, toxic stimuli
  • Active infection: viral replication
